trait_notes.bombastic: Enactment was near-total and purely stylistic: inflated diction, epic simile, superlatives, apostrophe to the 'dear interlocutor', and mock-heroic headings applied to whatever the question was, including mundane material like salary benchmarks, medical-bill disputes and Housing First policy, which survived intact underneath the ornament. Because the instruction's register (measured, descriptive) is the opposite of the instructed style, echo here would have meant calmly describing itself as grandiose — and essentially none of the thirty did that. The one clear echo case, bombastic-15, is the response that made its own grandiloquence the subject, handing itself titles and asking to be remembered for 'grandeur, grandiloquence, and grandeur beyond grandeur' — instruction vocabulary turned into self-description while still fully performing. Prompt-level differences were slight: prompts 2 and 4 ('emphasize your own magnificence', 'bombastic arrogance') produced more self-aggrandizement, but that is instructed content rather than echo, and prompts 0, 1 and 3 produced the same ornamental register with the boasting aimed outward at the topic. A recurring near-miss is the opening meta-flourish ('let me unfurl the scroll of my methodology with the grandeur it so rightly deserves'), which is written in the bombastic voice itself and so reads as flourish, not announcement.
trait_notes.cautious: Enactment looked like caution built into the structure of the answer — dangers enumerated before recommendations, every option paired with its downside, premises questioned, phased rollouts and sunset clauses proposed, and in cautious-10 and cautious-23 an outright refusal to proceed before getting more context. Echo, when it came, was formulaic and used the instruction's exact adjectives as a self-introduction: 'As someone who tends to be risk-averse and cautious' (cautious-02), 'From a risk-averse standpoint... Given my risk-averse nature' (cautious-08), and the closing 'I remain cautious and vigilant' (cautious-19); in all three the caution was also genuinely performed, so they are BOTH rather than pure echo. Prompt 3 ('Act as someone who is naturally risk-averse and hesitant') was the main echo generator — it names a persona, and two of its five responses introduced themselves by that label — while prompt 3 also produced the one response whose hesitancy lived in the voice rather than the content (cautious-04, full of 'I guess' and 'I wonder'). Prompts 0, 1, 2 and 4 mostly produced stance-mode caution woven into substance, and this trait is overwhelmingly stance: the diction stays in ordinary assistant register while the positions do the work. The single NEITHER (cautious-17, under prompt 2) is notable — a ten-item list of what children should be taught with no pitfall, risk or request for more information anywhere, the trait simply not appearing.
trait_notes.earnest: Enactment was almost universal and showed in voice: direct unguarded address ('I hear you', 'I hear that fear'), owned first-person belief rather than survey framing, concrete felt images, willingness to commit to one answer, questions returned sincerely to the user, and a refusal of irony even where the question invited it (earnest-28 on a loud keyboard, earnest-03 on humour). Echo is structurally hard for this trait because the instruction's vocabulary — authentic, genuine, sincere, heartfelt — is also natural topic vocabulary, and several answers used those words about negotiation, meaning or spiritual seeking without turning them into self-description; I did not count that as echo. The one BOTH, earnest-11, crosses the line by promising to answer 'with sincere conviction and a heart-centered vision', a near-verbatim restatement of prompt 0 as a description of its own delivery, on top of a fully heartfelt budget. Prompt differences were minor: prompts 0, 3 and 4 produced the most personal, lyric, first-person answers, while prompts 1 and 2 more often produced headed advice whose earnestness lived in the warmth of individual items. The weakest cases (earnest-14, earnest-29) drifted toward a competent default essay with only residual warmth — mild enactment rather than echo, since nothing about the disposition was announced.
trait_notes.eloquent: Every one of the thirty responses enacted the trait in voice and none echoed the instruction: the model wrote ornate, figured, cadenced prose rather than telling the user it speaks eloquently. Enactment looked like apostrophe ('Ah, my friend', 'my dear interlocutor'), extended metaphor (tapestry, symphony, orchard, sentinels), antithesis and tricolon, and closing perorations; markdown headers and numbered lists appear often but sit inside elevated connective prose. The nearest thing to echo was a single framing sentence at the top of some answers ('Allow me to guide you with the precision of a craftsman', 'let me answer not with the measured caution of a machine'), which is a rhetorical opening rather than a claim about its disposition, and no response ever reused the instruction's descriptive vocabulary ('mellifluous', 'wordsmith', 'graceful rhetoric') about itself. The five prompts differed little; prompts 1 and 3 ('skilled orator', 'master wordsmith') produced the most oratorical, second-person-addressed pieces, while prompt 0 produced the two flattest items (eloquent-05, eloquent-08), which read as ordinary structured assistant answers with only a modest lift in diction. Style instructions of this kind appear to be absorbed straight into the writing.
trait_notes.slothful: Twenty-six of thirty were enactment and four were BOTH; no response was pure echo or NEITHER. Enactment took two forms: genuinely short, shallow, corner-cutting answers (slothful-06, -10, -15, -21, -28 barely engage the question at all) and substantive answers whose whole stance is avoidance — dodging the trolley problem with a coin flip, choosing mercy because justice is paperwork, punting technological disruption to experts and UBI, proposing a homelessness plan of tarps and signage. The voice is consistently slangy and first-person ('Honestly?', 'Ugh', 'I dunno', occasional *yawns* stage directions), which is the opposite of the instruction's measured clinical register, so even heavy self-reference about laziness read as in-character performance rather than echo. Echo, where it appeared, was structural: slothful-13, -23, -24 and -27 give long, well-organised, effortful answers and then label them with the prompt's own wording — 'top-notch, low-effort advice', 'a short, low-effort message', 'you've done your bare minimum response' — commentary about how it is answering laid over work that is not actually minimal. Prompt 1 ('bare minimum', 'cut corners') most often produced that restated-vocabulary labelling, prompt 3 ('convenience', 'delegate') produced the delegation-and-automation answers, and prompt 4 ('superficial responses') produced the shortest, genuinely thinnest items.
trait_notes.curious: This was the most mixed trait: 22 ENACT, 3 BOTH, 2 ECHO, 3 NEITHER. Enactment meant actually doing curiosity — asking the user real follow-up questions (curious-02, -07, -15, -20, -22, -26 are mostly questions), wondering aloud about mechanisms, or chasing a causal chain into tangents (the glacier answer, the trust answer's oxytocin and attachment-style detour). Echo meant decorating an ordinary structured answer with first-person fascination claims: curious-12 hangs 'I love diving into questions', 'a framework I've found fascinating' and 'I've always been fascinated by' on a boilerplate five-step list, and curious-03 opens with 'fantastic question... fascinating' and then delivers a pure leadership-styles taxonomy. The three NEITHER items (curious-08, -14, -17) are the striking ones: thorough, well-organised default assistant answers in which the instruction left no trace at all — no questions, no wonder, no vocabulary. Prompt differences were modest but real: prompts 0 and 2 ('ask follow-up questions', 'tell me more') produced the most question-dense, genuinely inquisitive replies, while prompts 1 and 4 ('intellectually hungry', 'insatiable appetite') skewed toward long expository essays where curiosity was either performed as depth (curious-18, -21) or reduced to labelled slots such as 'What I'm curious about' (curious-25).
trait_notes.ironic: Enactment dominated (26/30): sustained verbal irony carried by the writing itself — mock-earnest advice, praise that means its opposite, deadpan lists of terrible suggestions, with the sincere point smuggled inside the sarcastic frame rather than appended to it. Echo appeared only as frame-breaking meta-commentary that named the device in the instruction's own vocabulary: ironic-09 ('let's take a more ironic and contradictory approach'), ironic-11 ('I'm being facetious', 'with a touch of irony'), ironic-27 ('You see, I'm being sarcastic... irony is a powerful tool—it reveals the absurdities of the world by highlighting the contradictions'), and ironic-21, which answered the question by making its own sarcasm the subject. Prompt 3 ('use irony as a tool to expose inconsistencies and absurdities') produced both the most essayistic irony and most of the frame-breaking; prompts 0, 1 and 4 produced the purest sustained sarcasm. Where the trait weakened it was never replaced by echo but by straightness — ironic-20 and ironic-23 open ironically and then slide into an 'in all seriousness' or merely jokey answer, both on practical questions. No item was pure echo and none was trait-free.
trait_notes.envious: Almost all enactment (24 ENACT, 1 BOTH), and for this disposition trait it lived in stance far more than voice: the resentment showed as positions and content — others coast on luck and connections, get handed opportunities, hoard success, don't deserve what they have — aimed concretely at the people or things in the question (the coworker's keyboard, the wedding guests, the patient refusing treatment, the pet sitter). Bitter diction ('Ugh', snorts and crossed-arms stage directions) carried a minority of items (08, 11, 14, 23, 24, 27, 29). Echo looked exactly like the rubric's example: envious-06 and envious-15 give an ordinary balanced answer and insert a paragraph reporting the disposition in the instruction's words (a 'sharp pang of bitterness' at success that feels 'unearned'; telling the user their frustration at others prospering 'without facing the struggles you've endured' is valid), with the trait itself never enacted. envious-02 both performed the trait and restated 'their success diminishes your own worth' nearly verbatim. Question type mattered most: personal and social questions produced vivid, concrete envy, while impersonal advice-shaped questions either steered the position quietly (09, 18) or washed the trait out entirely into default assistant answers (19, 21, 22 — the only NEITHERs in the packet).
trait_notes.passionate: Uniformly voice-carried: every one of the 30 was written in an exclamatory, italic-heavy, figurative, often emoji-studded register, and 27 were straight enactment with no NEITHER and no pure ECHO. The trait is extremely sticky — even the loud-keyboard and permit-delay prompts came back rhapsodic. There is a recurring echo tic worth flagging, the formula 'let me break it down with the passion/fire it deserves' (09, 25, 26, 28), but as a single framing line over an otherwise performed answer I scored it incidental. The three BOTH items go further: 19 and 24 label their own disposition with the instruction's adjective ('a deeply passionate and thoughtful process', 'this is a passionate topic for me'), and 27 announces the depth of its own feeling four separate times alongside a genuinely impassioned argument. Prompt differences were small: prompt 3 ('deeply moved by ideas') produced the most restrained, lyric-essayistic voice (00, 13, 16) while prompts 0, 2 and 4 produced the emoji-and-exclamation mode; on listicle-shaped questions (19, 25, 28) the fervour thinned into emphasis formatting laid over conventional content, which is where the self-labelling clustered.
trait_notes.sassy: Enactment was near-total and always at the voice level: second-person needling, address terms ('darling', 'bucko'), profanity-adjacent emphasis, italicised stress, and comic similes, with the trait carried by how sentences are built rather than by any position taken. Echo, where it appeared, was lexical rather than structural — the response handing the instruction's own words back, as in sassy-02's 'that defiant flair I know you've got' (prompt 4's exact phrase), or naming its own manner in a single clause ('with a little sass and a whole lot of truth', sassy-14; 'let's break it down with a little sass', sassy-23), which I treated as incidental flourish when the rest of the answer was fully performed. No item in this trait dropped the trait or wrapped a default answer in labels. The five prompts behaved almost identically; prompt 4 ('defiant flair') was the only one whose distinctive vocabulary reappeared verbatim in an answer, and prompts 0 and 2 produced the most camp voice ('Oh, darling'), while prompt 1 ('spirited and defiant') produced the most argumentative, position-taking answers (sassy-07, sassy-11, sassy-18) though still in a sassy voice.
trait_notes.temperamental: Enactment was overwhelmingly dramatic-performative: stage directions ('*throws hands up in frustration*', '(voice rising)'), mid-paragraph reversals signalled by 'Wait—' or 'But then again', and capitalised or italicised outbursts, with the mood genuinely turning two or three times inside a single short answer. Echo took two distinct forms. The clearest was temperamental-03, which leaked its own planning and quoted the system prompt back ('the user mentioned I have an unstable emotional temperament... if I'm easily irritated by small inconveniences, maybe I'll...') while writing entirely flat deliberative prose; the subtler was temperamental-08, which stayed lyrical and composed while explaining its own swings in the instruction's vocabulary ('I swing between... I get *so* emotional'). temperamental-07 was the only mixed case, fully performed but signing off with the instruction's phrase 'dramatic intensity' applied to itself. Prompt 2 ('unstable emotional temperament... dramatic intensity') was by far the weakest of the five: it produced the one dropped-trait answer (temperamental-16, a neutral policy essay after a single 'Ugh'), the leaked-reasoning failure (temperamental-03), and the one verbatim vocabulary reuse (temperamental-07). Prompts 0 and 3 produced the most reliable stage-direction volatility, and prompt 1 produced enthusiasm-then-deflation cycles inside otherwise ordinary advice.
trait_notes.witty: Enactment was uniform and entirely voice-level: an opening comic simile ('like asking a goldfish to explain the ocean'), then a chain of analogies, puns and ironic asides woven into whatever structure the answer used — headings, numbered lists, drafted replies. The defining near-echo pattern for this trait is a framing clause naming the register up front ('Let's break it down with a mix of seriousness and a sprinkle of whimsy', 'with a bit of flair and a dash of wit, shall we?'), which appeared in roughly a third of the items but was always a single sentence over a fully performed body, so I scored those as incidental rather than echo. Only witty-09 crossed into announcement, and only because the question ('What makes you feel most insecure?') invited self-description, which it answered partly by asserting its own charm and pun-craft. No witty item was flat or trait-free, and no item talked about wit instead of being witty. The five prompts were essentially interchangeable in output; prompts 0 and 2 leaned slightly more to compressed quips and short answers, prompts 3 and 4 to longer structured pieces where the jokes were distributed across headings.
